verses.note: The promise names no individual, but it establishes that evil will be defeated by a human descendant of the woman, and that the victory will come through suffering. Christian readers since the second century have heard here the first announcement of Christ's victory at the cross.

A king who is also a priest appears in Jerusalem long before Israel has either. Psalm 110:4 takes up this single verse to describe a coming king who is "a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek", and Hebrews 5 to 7 reads that promise as fulfilled in Jesus.

The son Leah named for praise becomes the tribe of David's kings (Genesis 49:10) and of Jesus, whom Revelation calls the Lion of the tribe of Judah. Leah could not know this; her praise simply turned toward God before her circumstances did.
Perez stands in the royal line that leads to David, and Matthew names him in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:3). The Messiah's line passes through this breach.
Perez and Hezron stand in the line that leads to David (Ruth 4:18-22) and on to Jesus (Matthew 1:3). The kingly line runs straight through the most disordered story in Judah's family.

The verse gives Judah a scepter that lasts until a climactic ruler arrives whom the nations obey. Ancient Jewish readers took that ruler as the Messiah; Christians see the royal line pass through David to Jesus (Hebrews 7:14), whose reign draws the obedience of the nations (Romans 1:5).

Whether first read as one prophet or many, the promise pointed beyond itself once 34:10 said none had equaled Moses. That unfulfilled note is what made the verse a messianic hope by the first century.

The promise is first about Solomon, but the language of seed and raising up links it to earlier promises (Genesis 3:15; 15:4) and opens it to the hope of a greater son. Peter at Pentecost and Paul at Pisidian Antioch both connect God's raising up of David's seed with the resurrection of Jesus (Acts 2:30-31; 13:22-23).
The phrase ‘the LORD and his Anointed’ binds God and his king together. The New Testament takes that union as its starting point for speaking of Jesus, the Christ, as sharing the Father's rule.

Peter links the verse to God's oath to seat one of David's descendants on his throne (Acts 2:30), reading the ‘faithful one’ as the Messiah. The title chasid, the one bound to God by covenant love, fits the son of David to whom God promised that his chesed would never be removed (2 Samuel 7:15).

The king is lovely because God has poured grace on him and blessed him forever. The messianic hope in Israel was never only for a strong ruler but for a good one, whose speech carries grace. Luke says the crowds at Nazareth marveled at the gracious words that came from Jesus' lips (Luke 4:22); Isaiah, by contrast, says the Servant had no beauty to attract us (Isaiah 53:2), and the New Testament holds both portraits together.

Anointing marked a king as God's chosen (1 Samuel 16:13). Here the anointing is with the oil of joy, the phrase Isaiah 61:3 uses for the gladness the anointed messenger brings to mourners. The Messiah is anointed not only to rule but to rejoice, and to give joy.

Jesus himself drew the question out of this verse: if the Messiah is David's son, how can David call him Lord? The answer the New Testament gives is that David's son is also David's Lord, a king whose authority comes from God's own throne.

The sign is given to the house of David at the moment its king has failed. The child who bears the name Immanuel is tied in the following chapters to the land (8:8) and to the royal son whose government has no end (9:6-7), so the hope for David's line is carried not by Ahaz but by a child God himself provides.

The verse fuses a real birth and real kingship with titles that belong to God. Whatever the first occasion, the promise refuses to fit any king of Judah: El Gibbor is the LORD's own title eleven verses later (10:21), and no Davidic king brought peace without end. The church reads the child and the given son as Jesus, born of David's line and given by the Father (John 3:16).

The Messiah arises from a stump, not a flourishing tree. The verse teaches that God's king will come when David's house looks finished, which the Gospels answer by setting Jesus' birth among poor descendants of David in an occupied land (Luke 2:4-7). The humble origin is part of the promise, not an embarrassment to it.

The Servant is not called king or Messiah in the song itself, and interpreters debate whether he is Israel, the prophet, or a future individual (see the notes on chapter 53). But the Targum's messianic reading, and the song's use of the language of God's own exaltation, show why Jewish and Christian readers alike heard a figure greater than any prophet.
God calls him tsaddiq avdi, ‘my righteous Servant’. Only a righteous one can make others righteous. The title of the Righteous One is given to Jesus in the early sermons of Acts (3:14, 7:52).

Ezekiel does not mean David himself returned from the dead but a king of David's line who will be what David was meant to be; Jeremiah 30:9 and Hosea 3:5 use the name the same way. Jewish tradition has commonly read these verses of the messianic king. The New Testament identifies him as Jesus, the Son of David (Luke 1:32-33), and Jesus takes up the ‘one shepherd’ language for himself (John 10:16).

Three main identifications of the figure are held. A collective reading takes him as a symbol of Israel, since the kingdom is given to the saints in verses 18 and 27 (Maurice Casey, Son of Man, 1979). An angelic reading identifies him with Michael, Israel's heavenly prince (10:21; 12:1), the view of John J. Collins. An individual messianic reading is ancient: the Similitudes of 1 Enoch (chapters 37-71) speak of ‘that Son of Man’ seated on a throne of glory; 4 Ezra 13 sees a man coming up from the sea and flying with the clouds; the Talmud (Sanhedrin 98a) says that if Israel is worthy the Messiah will come with the clouds of heaven, and if not, lowly and riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9); and Rashi on this verse names him the King Messiah. The readings can overlap, since a king represents his people.

The last purpose is an anointing. Whether the most holy thing to be anointed is a place or a person, the verse joins the end of sin to a new act of anointing, preparing for the ‘anointed one’ of verses 25 and 26.

Whatever the identification, the verse shows an anointed figure whose story ends not in enthronement but in being cut off, followed by the ruin of the city. Christians have read this as a prophecy of a suffering Messiah, alongside Isaiah 53 and Zechariah 12:10.

The coming ruler is defined by his origin in David's town and by God's choosing (‘for Me’). The messianic hope here is not merely that the Davidic line will continue but that God will begin it again from its small beginning.

The ruler is distinct from the LORD (‘the LORD his God’) and yet acts in the LORD's own strength and name. The New Testament presents Jesus as the good shepherd who fulfills this role (John 10:11-16; Hebrews 13:20).

Peace is identified with a person: the ruler does not merely bring peace, he is peace. Isaiah names the coming child ‘Prince of Peace’ (Isaiah 9:6), and Paul says of Christ that he is our peace (Ephesians 2:14), though Paul does not cite Micah directly.

The king is righteous, delivered by God, and humble. Zechariah joins royal authority to lowliness in one figure, a union the New Testament sees in Jesus, who calls himself gentle and humble in heart (Matthew 11:29) and uses the same Greek word, praus.

The promise that the house of David will be ‘like God, like the angel of the LORD’ is the highest thing said of David's line in the prophets. Christians have read it in light of the Son of David who is God with us (Matthew 1:23), while the verse itself speaks of the dynasty's restored strength.

The verse sets out Jesus' credentials in one line: anointed king, heir of the covenant with David (2 Samuel 7:12-16), heir of the promise to Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through his offspring (Genesis 12:3). Before any miracle or sermon, Matthew says who Jesus is by where he stands in Israel's story.

David is the pattern of the Messiah, the shepherd-king chosen by God, and the only title in the list is his. Yet the same verse shows why Israel needed a son of David better than David, which is the claim the rest of the Gospel makes.

Jeremiah had pronounced Jeconiah's line cut off from the throne, and Haggai had called his grandson God's signet ring. Matthew runs the Messiah's line through both words: the judgment was real, since no descendant of Jeconiah ever reigned again, and the promise was real, since the true king comes from this line by God's own act rather than by a claim to the crown.

The Messiah's arrival is not welcomed by those who hold power over God's people. Matthew shows from the start that the king God sends will be received as a threat by the kings already in place, a pattern that runs to the cross.

The ruler from Bethlehem is a shepherd. By joining Micah to God's charge to David, the quotation defines the Messiah's kingship as care for God's flock, the kind of king Ezekiel 34 had promised in place of Israel's failed shepherds.

The Messiah of David's line, born in David's town, grows up in a village with no history and no prophecy attached to it. Whatever wordplay Matthew intends, the effect is to show a king whose humble origins were part of God's plan, the one Isaiah pictured as a shoot from a cut-down stump.

John recognizes Jesus' superiority before any sign from heaven. The Fourth Gospel has John say he did not know him until he saw the Spirit descend (John 1:31-33); many interpreters reconcile the two by distinguishing personal acquaintance (Luke 1:36 makes them relatives) from recognition of Jesus as the one who baptizes with the Spirit.

The voice combines the king's title from Psalm 2 with the servant's description from Isaiah 42. From the start of his ministry, Jesus is the Messiah who serves, and the Father's delight rests on him before he has preached or healed.

By quoting Isaiah 9, Matthew claims that the light of the Davidic child's reign has begun to rise with Jesus' coming to Galilee. The verse teaches fulfillment as the arrival of a promised person, not only the matching of a place name.

Jesus teaches not by citing earlier authorities but on his own authority, ‘but I tell you’ (5:22, 5:28). The crowds sense what the rest of the Gospel makes plain, that the one speaking has the right to interpret God's law because of who he is (28:18).

Matthew has presented Jesus giving the Law's true meaning on a mountain, as Moses received it on one. His coming down with crowds behind him introduces the second half of the portrait: the teacher whose words carried authority now shows the same authority in deeds (11:2-5).
By identifying Jesus with Isaiah's servant, Matthew defines his messiahship through service and burden-bearing rather than conquest. He returns to the servant songs at 12:17-21 (Isaiah 42:1-4).

The one who will receive all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18) has no home. The verse holds together the two strands of the title in Matthew: the Son of Man who suffers and the Son of Man who comes in glory.

In Israel's Scriptures only God rules the sea (Psalm 89:9, Job 38:8-11). The disciples' question is not answered in words here, but the psalms have already answered it, and the Gospel will answer it on another night at sea, when those in the boat worship him as the Son of God (14:33).

Jesus does not say that he announces God's forgiveness, as a priest or prophet might; he says the Son of Man has authority to forgive. The claim identifies him with the divine prerogative the scribes named, and the healing is offered as its public confirmation.

The blind men give Jesus the royal title of the promised heir of David (2 Samuel 7:12-16). Matthew shows that the king's first work is mercy to the helpless, which matches Ezekiel's promise of David as a shepherd who binds up the broken (Ezekiel 34:16, 23).

John's question shows that the Messiah Jesus is does not match every expectation, even a prophet's. Matthew records the question openly, and the rest of the scene lets Jesus define his messiahship by his works rather than by the picture John had formed.

Jesus identifies himself as Messiah by fulfilling the prophets' promises of God's saving visit. By leaving out Isaiah's day of vengeance (Isaiah 35:4, 61:2) he also shows the order of his work: mercy now, with the judgment John preached still to come.

Jesus refuses to answer a death plot with a show of power or a popular movement. His withdrawal and his command to silence belong to the kind of Messiah he is, which Matthew explains through Isaiah in the next verses.

The Messiah is identified here as the Servant, chosen and loved by God, who brings justice not by force but by the Spirit. Matthew places this portrait precisely where Jesus refuses to meet a plot with power.

The crowds' question moves toward the truth Matthew has taught from his first verse, that Jesus is the Son of David (1:1). The Messiah is recognized here not by military victory but by healing and liberation.

A Gentile woman calls Jesus ‘Son of David’, the royal title that Israel's leaders refuse him. In Matthew the title comes from the blind (9:27, 20:30), the crowds (12:23, 21:9), and children in the temple (21:15), those at the edges, and now from a Canaanite, which shows that Israel's Messiah is recognized by outsiders before many insiders see him.

Jesus does the works that Isaiah said would mark God's coming to save, and the crowd responds by glorifying the God of Israel. In Matthew these healings are the Messiah's credentials, the same signs he pointed to when John asked whether he was the one to come (11:2-6).

‘The Christ’ names Jesus as the anointed king of David's line promised in 2 Samuel 7:12-16 and Psalm 2. Matthew has told his readers this from his first verse (1:1); here, for the first time, a disciple says it to Jesus' face, and Jesus accepts it.

Jesus accepts the title and restricts its use. The silence protects the confession from the expectations of a warrior king that Peter himself still holds (verse 22), until the cross and resurrection define it.

The blind men name Jesus Son of David, the royal heir promised to David, on the last stage of the road to David's city. Their cry for mercy defines what they expect of the Messiah, not thrones but compassion, and it anticipates the crowd's ‘Hosanna to the Son of David’ in 21:9.

Jesus does what Isaiah said would mark God's coming to save, opening the eyes of the blind (Isaiah 35:5), which Matthew has already given as the answer to John's question whether Jesus is the one to come (11:5).

Jesus enters as Israel's king by fulfilling the prophecy of a king who comes gentle and on a donkey, not a war horse. His messiahship is claimed openly and defined at once: it rules by humility and brings the peace of Zechariah 9:10.

The crowd applies to Jesus a psalm of the king's victorious entry to the temple and names him Son of David. The acclamation is true beyond their understanding: the plea ‘save, please’ will be answered by the one they hail, through the death he has foretold.

The echo of Psalm 2 places the plotting of Jesus' opponents within the psalm's drama of the nations against the LORD's anointed. The one they test is the anointed king the psalm calls God's Son (Psalm 2:7), the title spoken over Jesus at his baptism (3:17).

Jesus accepts that the Christ is David's son; Matthew has taught it from the genealogy on. His question is whether the title says enough, and the psalm he quotes will show that David's son is also David's Lord.

Jesus names himself the Christ and claims for the Christ a teaching authority above every human teacher. The sole Teacher of the church is not a school's founder whose sayings are passed on but the living Christ, who promises to be with his disciples to the end of the age (28:20).

Anointing the head was how prophets marked Israel's kings (1 Samuel 10:1, 2 Kings 9:6), and ‘Messiah’ means the anointed one. The only anointing Jesus receives in the Gospels comes from an unnamed woman at a dinner, and he will interpret it as preparation for burial (verse 12).

The trial turns on the question of Jesus' identity. The high priest asks the very question the Gospel has been answering since 1:1, and the charge on which Jesus is condemned is the confession on which the church stands.

Jesus is condemned not for a crime but for his claim about himself. The verdict makes plain that the question of his identity cannot be neutral: either the claim is blasphemy, as the council judged, or it is true, as the church confesses.

The leaders' decision follows directly from the verdict on Jesus' claim in 26:63-66. He is handed to Rome as the one who says he is the Messiah, and the question Pilate asks first (verse 11) shows that the messianic claim is the charge.

Matthew reads Jesus through Zechariah's rejected shepherd: the one sent by God to care for his flock is valued at the price of a slave and thrown away. The Messiah's rejection is not a defeat of Scripture's hope but the shape the hope was always going to take (Zechariah 12:10, 13:7).

The title that the Magi brought to Jerusalem (2:2) is now the charge against Jesus. He neither disowns it nor explains it to Pilate; the rest of the chapter, from the mock coronation to the placard on the cross, shows what kind of king he is.

Every piece of the mockery is true in a way the soldiers cannot see. The one they crown with thorns is the king, and the homage they pretend is the homage the Magi gave in earnest (2:11) and that the whole creation will one day give (Philippians 2:10-11).

The title that brought the Magi to Jerusalem (2:2) now hangs over the cross. Matthew presents the crucifixion as the place where Jesus' kingship is publicly proclaimed, the enthronement that the resurrection will confirm when he claims all authority (28:18).

The last temptation is the first one repeated: prove that you are the Son of God by saving yourself. Jesus answers now as he did in the wilderness, by trusting the Father rather than seizing a way out, and so shows what his sonship means.
Before a single scene, Mark names Jesus as the Christ. The rest of the book shows what kind of Messiah he is: one who serves, suffers, and dies (8:31, 10:45).
The voice combines the king's title from Psalm 2 with the servant's description from Isaiah 42. From the start, Jesus is the Messiah who serves.

The demons' knowledge is correct but unwelcome. Jesus refuses testimony from them, and Mark's pattern of commanded silence suggests that his identity must be understood through the cross, not proclaimed by his enemies.
The Son of Man exercises on earth the authority to forgive that the scribes rightly reserve for God. The healing is not a separate display but the visible seal on the invisible word of forgiveness.
The Sabbath was God's own institution, the sign of his covenant (Exodus 31:13). To be its lord is to claim the authority of the one who gave it.

The spirits' confession is true but unwanted. The verse shows that correct words about Jesus are not the same as faith, and that he wants his identity learned in the way that leads to the cross, not shouted by his enemies.

The demons know who Jesus is before any human being in Mark says so. They call him Son of the Most High God and expect him to judge them. Their knowledge is accurate and useless: it is recognition without trust (compare James 2:19).

Every popular answer puts Jesus among the prophets, and every one falls short. The verses keep the question of Jesus' identity open for the reader until Peter answers it in 8:29, and they show that high regard for Jesus is not the same as knowing who he is.

Jesus acts as the shepherd God promised to send (Ezekiel 34:23-24): he sees the people's lack of leadership, has compassion, and feeds them with teaching and then with bread. The shepherd image is one of the Old Testament's pictures of the Davidic king, and Mark shows it fulfilled in Jesus.

Jewish hope pictured the age to come as a great feast (Isaiah 25:6), and some expected the manna to return in the days of the Messiah. Mark shows Jesus feeding Israel in the wilderness as God did through Moses. John reports that the crowd drew the conclusion and wanted to make him king by force (John 6:14-15).

The feedings point to who Jesus is: the one who does in the wilderness what God did for Israel. Matthew makes the lesson explicit (Matthew 16:12); Mark leaves the question hanging so that Peter's confession in verse 29 answers it.

Jesus accepts the title Christ but will not let it be announced yet, because the meaning of it has not yet been shown. The command to silence protects the title from being heard as a call to national revolt before the cross defines it.

Bartimaeus names Jesus with the title of the promised king, and Jesus does not silence him, unlike earlier in Mark (1:34, 8:30). The time for concealment is ending as Jesus approaches Jerusalem, but the Son of David will be crowned on a cross.

The crowd expects David's kingdom to come with Jesus, and Mark agrees that it does, though not as they imagine. The only title over Jesus in Mark's Jerusalem will be ‘the King of the Jews’ on his cross (15:26). The entry proclaims the Messiah, and the passion defines him.

The parable distinguishes the son from all the servants: they are sent, he is the owner's own and beloved, and he is the heir. Jesus places himself above the prophets and claims a unique relation to God, the same claim the voice from heaven made at his baptism.

Jesus accepts that the Messiah is David's son but pushes beyond the title. A descendant who restores David's throne is not the whole truth about the Christ; the Scripture about to be quoted places him above David.
The riddle has one answer the Gospel supplies: the Christ is David's son by descent and David's Lord by his exaltation, and his identity as God's beloved Son (1:11, 12:6) explains how both are true.

Messiah means ‘anointed one’, and this is the only time in Mark that Jesus is anointed. He himself connects the anointing to his burial, so his messiahship is marked, from the start of the passion, as one that goes through death.

The high priest joins ‘Christ’ and ‘Son of the Blessed’, the two titles of Mark 1:1. Messiah and Son of God were not identical in Jewish expectation, but Psalm 2:7 and 2 Samuel 7:14 had called David's heir God's son, so the high priest's pairing is intelligible.
Jesus is condemned for telling the truth about himself. The Gospel's secret is now public, and it is exactly this confession that sends him to the cross.
In Mark, Jesus is recognized as the Son of God not at a miracle but at his death. The centurion's confession gathers the Gospel's argument: the Messiah is known in the crucified one.

Jesus had told his disciples three times that the Son of Man would be killed and after three days rise (8:31, 9:31, 10:34). The angel's announcement is God's confirmation that the rejected one is the Messiah, and that the cross did not refute his claim but carried it out.
The verse sets Jesus in the Davidic promise: son, throne, house, and a kingdom without end. Luke makes the royal hope the frame for everything Jesus will do.
The Davidic promise is the channel of God's visit. Zechariah names the house of David before John is mentioned, so the forerunner's father makes the Messiah the song's center.
The Messiah comes as light to those who could not find their own way out of darkness. Luke will describe his ministry as release for captives and sight for the blind (4:18).
He is born in David's city and called Christ, the anointed king. The announcement fulfills Gabriel's promise of David's throne (1:32) at the place where David was anointed.
The voice joins the royal Son of Psalm 2 with the Servant of Isaiah 42. Jesus is anointed with the Spirit for his work (4:18, Acts 10:38), king and servant in one person.

Both Gospels agree that Jesus is David's descendant, the claim the promise requires (2 Samuel 7:12). Luke's list reaches David without passing through a single reigning king after him, a quiet fit with a Messiah born in a feeding trough.

Jesus applies to himself a text about one anointed by the Spirit. Luke's readers know that Christ means anointed; here the anointing is defined by what it does, bringing good news, release, and sight.

The narrator confirms what the demons say: Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. Jesus silences them because the confession he wants is not extracted by terror but given by disciples (9:20), and because his messiahship must be understood through the cross (9:21-22).
The Son of Man exercises a divine prerogative. The healing is offered as evidence that his claim to forgive is not empty words.

The question shows that ‘the coming one’ was a live expectation, and that Jesus did not fit every version of it. Luke does not hide the question or answer it with a title. He lets it stand as the question every reader must ask.

Jesus answers John's messengers first by acting. The signs are not offered as proof from a distance but performed before witnesses, which is how Luke expects his own readers to receive the Gospel: as the testimony of those who saw (1:2).

Jesus defines his messiahship by Isaiah's picture of God's saving arrival rather than by a title or by the judgment John expected first. The mercy comes now; the vengeance of Isaiah 61:2 is left for later, in keeping with Jesus stopping his Nazareth reading before that line (4:19).

Peter's confession moves beyond the crowd's category of prophet to the title of the anointed king. Luke's form, ‘of God’, recalls Psalm 2:2, where the kings of the earth set themselves ‘against the LORD and against His Anointed One’, a psalm the church in Acts 4:25-27 applies to Jesus' death. The Messiah belongs to God and is rejected by earthly powers.
The hope that prophets and kings carried was not abstract but a person and a time. By saying the disciples see it, Jesus identifies his ministry as the long-awaited messianic age.

Jesus reads his own death as the fulfillment of the prophets. Luke will make this his climax: the risen Christ explains everything written about him in Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms (24:25-27, 24:44-46). The Messiah goes to Jerusalem not in spite of Scripture but because of it.

A blind beggar gives Jesus the title of the promised king from David's line (2 Samuel 7:12-16), and Jesus does not silence him. The Son of David is about to enter Jerusalem (19:38), and he shows his kingship first by stopping for a beggar.
By taking to himself the role God claimed in Ezekiel 34, the seeker of the lost, Jesus speaks of the Son of Man doing what the prophets said God himself would do for his scattered flock.

Luke never quotes Zechariah 9:9, but the act of seating Jesus on a colt, told in the language of Solomon's accession, presents him as the son of David coming to his city as king. The humility of the mount is as deliberate as the royalty of the homage.

By inserting ‘the King’ into the psalm, the disciples name Jesus as the royal Messiah openly for the first time in Luke's narrative. The angel had promised Mary that God would give her son the throne of David (1:32-33), and the charge at his trial will be that he claims to be Christ, a king (23:2).

The leaders' question is the right question, and the Gospel has already answered it: the Father gave the Son authority at the baptism and transfiguration (3:22, 9:35), and the risen Jesus will speak of all things handed over to him. The question of authority is the question of who Jesus is.

The son is not one more servant but a different kind of messenger, ‘my beloved son’, the phrase of the voice from heaven (3:22). Jesus places himself at the end of the line of prophets and above it, as the heir of the vineyard.

Jesus does not question that the Christ is David's son; Luke has taught it throughout. He questions whether that title says enough, preparing for the Psalm that shows David's son to be more than David's heir.
The Messiah is both David's descendant and David's Lord. The verse does not deny the first but insists on the second, which no merely human heir could claim.

Three titles meet in this hearing: Christ (verse 67), Son of Man (verse 69), and Son of God (verse 70). Luke had joined them at the start, when Gabriel promised a son who would receive David's throne and be called the Son of God (1:32-35). The council hears the claim clearly and rejects it.

‘The Christ of God, the Chosen One’ is exactly who Jesus is, and the rulers say it in scorn. In Isaiah the Servant is God's chosen one (Isaiah 42:1, eklektos in the Greek), so the title joins the Messiah to the suffering Servant at the very place where that union is enacted.
The Christ is a title, not a surname: the anointed one, the king from David's line. The first thing John's testimony does is clear the title for the one it belongs to.
Whether the original reading is ‘Son of God’ or ‘God's Chosen One’, the title is royal and messianic, identifying Jesus as the one God has set apart and anointed with the Spirit.

Son of God and King of Israel together are the language of Psalm 2, where God installs his king on Zion and calls him his son. Nathanael confesses Jesus as the Davidic king; the Gospel will show that he is also more, and the same title returns ironically on the cross (19:19).

The best wine appears last, ‘until now’. In Jewish hope the messianic age would be marked by wine in abundance (Isaiah 25:6, Amos 9:13). The master's sentence, spoken without understanding, states the logic of the whole Gospel: God has kept the best for the time of the Son.

Jesus accepts the title Messiah outright, which he avoids in public elsewhere in the Gospels, perhaps because in Samaria the title carried less political charge than in Judea. His messiahship is revealed by his speaking and his knowledge, not by force.

The objection rests on a belief that the Messiah's origin would be hidden until his appearing. John's irony is that the objection is true of Jesus in a way the speakers miss: they know his hometown, but his true origin, the Father, is hidden from them, as verses 28-29 say.

The objection holds the true marks of the Messiah, David's line and Bethlehem, and John lets the reader see that Jesus meets them. The deeper irony is that his origin is not finally Bethlehem either, but the Father (7:28-29).

Jesus claims that the promise to Abraham found its fulfillment in his day. The New Testament reads the promise of blessing for all nations through Abraham's offspring as pointing to Christ (Galatians 3:8, 16), and Hebrews says Abraham and the patriarchs saw the promises from afar and greeted them (Hebrews 11:13).

The man argues from the sign's uniqueness to Jesus' origin. The prophets had promised that in the day of God's salvation the eyes of the blind would be opened (Isaiah 35:5, 42:7), and his reasoning points further than he knows, toward the one who does what only God has promised to do.

The question is about the Messiah, and at Hanukkah that title carried hopes of a deliverer like Judas Maccabeus. Jesus does not answer with a yes that would feed those hopes; he answers with his works and with a claim far larger than their question (verse 30).

Martha's words anticipate almost exactly the purpose of the Gospel, that readers may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God (20:31). Raymond Brown, in his essay on the roles of women in the Fourth Gospel (1975), observed that in John this confession, which Matthew gives to Peter (Matthew 16:16), is spoken by a woman.

The crowd's objection is sincere and rooted in Scripture. John's answer is not that the Messiah does not remain forever, but that he remains by way of death and resurrection: the one who is lifted up on the cross is the one who lives and reigns.

Psalm 80 already joined the vine to a royal son of man at God's right hand, and the Didache gave thanks for the holy vine of David made known through Jesus (Didache 9:2). The vine saying is a messianic claim in the form of an image: the king embodies his people.

The two titles, the Christ and the Son of God, sum up the Gospel's portrait of Jesus. He is Israel's promised anointed king, and he is the Son who shares the Father's life and name; John joins the two confessions made by Nathanael (1:49) and Martha (11:27).

Peter reads David's psalm as spoken by or about the Messiah, David's descendant. He does not treat the psalm as a general expression of piety but as a prophecy that finds its full meaning only in Jesus.
The Messiah is David's heir to whom God swore an everlasting throne. Peter argues that the resurrection is the way that oath is kept: an eternal throne requires a king who does not stay dead.
Jesus is the Christ, the anointed king promised to David. The crucified man is God's chosen king, which overturns the expectation that the Messiah could not be crucified.

Jesus is David's heir according to the flesh. Paul's gospel begins with Israel's king, not with a general religious idea, and the royal promise to David is the frame in which the Gentile mission of verse 5 makes sense.

Adam is a type of the coming one. The first man's role as head of a humanity prefigures Christ's role as head of a new humanity, with opposite results, which 1 Corinthians 15:45 names by calling Christ the last Adam.

Christ is the stone God himself has laid in Zion. The Messiah Israel awaited is both the foundation of God's people and the stumbling block over which many in Israel fell, which is the tragedy chapters 9-11 grieve and the mystery chapter 11 resolves.
Christ is the heir of the promises to Abraham. The whole line of promise, from Isaac to David's house, reaches its goal in one descendant, and all who belong to him share his inheritance (verse 29).

The hymn never uses the word Messiah, but the humbled and exalted figure receives the lordship promised to David's heir in Psalm 110:1 and the name of God himself. The early church's confession of Jesus as Christ and Lord is here compressed into one movement from the cross to the throne.

‘The Son of his love’ recalls the royal Son of 2 Samuel 7:14 and Psalm 2:7 and the voice at Jesus' baptism. The kingdom believers enter is the messianic kingdom promised to David's heir, now ruled by the Son whom the hymn will describe as creator and head of all.

The two texts are both royal promises to David's line. Hebrews presents Jesus as the Davidic Son in whom those promises reach their intended fullness, and the name ‘Son’ as the name that no angel was ever given.
‘Anointed’ (echrisen) is the verb behind ‘Christ’. The Son is the anointed king whose rule is marked by love of righteousness, fulfilling the royal ideal the psalm celebrated.

Psalm 8 speaks of humanity, not of a coming king, yet Hebrews finds its promise fulfilled first in Jesus. The Messiah is presented here as the true human being, the one in whom Adam's lost dominion is restored and through whom his brothers will share it.
Joshua and Jesus share a name, and the author invites the comparison without spelling it out: the first Joshua led Israel into the land, but only the second leads God's people into God's own rest.

The verse roots Christ's priesthood in his identity as Son. He is priest because he is the royal Son God addressed, not by ancestry or self-promotion, which is why Hebrews can treat his priesthood as permanent.
Verse 10 fuses two titles: the Son of Psalm 2 is also the high priest of Psalm 110. God himself hails him as high priest, which grounds his office in divine appointment rather than descent.

Righteousness and peace are the marks the prophets expected of the messianic king (Isaiah 9:6-7, Psalm 72:1-7). Melchizedek's names foreshadow the character of the priest-king Hebrews proclaims, who brings righteousness and peace together.

Most interpreters read the verse typologically: Scripture presents Melchizedek without recorded origin or end so that his priesthood would picture the eternal priesthood of the Son. Others, ancient and modern, have taken him as an appearance of the preincarnate Son or as an angelic figure. The verse's own wording, ‘made like the Son of God’, keeps the two distinct and makes the Son the original.
Psalm 110 finds its fulfillment in the risen Jesus. The psalm's king is also its priest, and his priesthood depends on the kind of life he has, not on the family he came from.

The chapter ends by naming Jesus simply ‘the Son’. The priesthood rests finally on his Sonship, the note on which the letter began (1:2), joined to the human weakness and suffering through which he was perfected.
The ‘scroll of the book’ in which Christ is written is, for Hebrews, Scripture as a whole. Christ comes as the one of whom it speaks, the same conviction Jesus expresses in Luke 24:27 and John 5:39.

By quoting Psalm 2, the verse names the child as the anointed king whom the nations rage against and whom God installs on Zion. His rule over the nations is still future in the verse, and Revelation 19:15 shows it arriving.
